items.title: "And You Would be Supporting a Local Paper"
items.author: Aphyr
items.content:
Last spring my dear friend Taber was doored while riding his bike, and came very close to dying. A friend and I got in our cars, made it to the hospital by three AM, and spent the next week caring for him. We traded off sitting at his bedside, making sure he stayed plugged in to the machines keeping him alive, coordinating with a dozen-odd specialists, taking notes, working with the medical and city bureaucracy, and transitioning to home care. My client was kind enough to let me take some time off, but I was still trying to work my way through a slew of database bugs during spare moments. We stayed in a hotel best described as “backrooms”, and I picked up a case of scabies. There was one point where I started crying while trying to pick out thank-you cards at Target. It was, in short, an exceedingly rough time, and it took the better part of a month to really recover.

Taber, thank goodness, has made a spectacular recovery, and I’m so happy for him. My friend who came to care for him was an incredible rock, and I couldn’t have asked for a more compassionate, diligent, and trustworthy partner. Our family and friends who took care of our homes and pets while we vanished—thank you so much. I’m deeply grateful to everyone at Hennepin County Medical Center, the first responders, the folks at the Minneapolis Public Services building, the care workers, and everyone who donated to help get him back on track. I was, and remain, deeply moved.

This is by far the more important story, but something else happened that week—something so surreal and deeply silly that I want to relate it as well. I started getting spam.

I mean, we all get spam. As someone who’s been around the net for a while, I get a of it. But these emails got through the filters, and came almost every day. They were all from the same guy, “Tom Santogato”. They had the obnoxious hallmarks of LLM slop. Between trying to get video footage from the city and buying medical equipment, I’d read:

Quick question, when was the last time you knew exactly what your brand truly makes on every dollar spent? Most DTC founders tell me they track CAC and margins, but the reality they act on is often off by enough to flip decisions.

That’s why I built something different: a free 45-minute Financial Diagnostic that calculates true unit economics, contribution margin, CAC, and first-order profitability the way investors would, live on screen.

Here’s what makes it powerful:

📌 Real vs reported metrics: we reconcile your Shopify + ad platform data the right way.

📊 Understand what you actually keep on every sale: after discounts, shipping, returns, processing, and fulfillment.

🚀 Turn insights into action: plan budgets, scale channels with confidence, or prep for growth/raising capital.

✔️ All live. All transparent. No dashboards to guess from, just clarity.

If this feels like the kind of visibility missing from your strategy, let’s book a time — zero risk, no commitment, just real metrics that move decisions.

Would Monday or Tuesday work better for you?

I clicked the unsubscribe link. I know this is usually a trap, but also, due diligence. They kept coming, of course.

I saw Woof posted about {{specific_hiring_initiative}} last week—and noticed your team has been actively engaging with hiring content over the past few days.

One thing we’ve found working with similar-sized teams: the biggest bottleneck in that phase isn’t usually finding candidates, it’s {{specific_pain_point_related_to_their_signal}}. Most teams don’t realize this until they’re 4-6 weeks in.

Not sure if that’s on your radar, but thought it was worth flagging given the timeline you’re working with.

Worth a quick conversation?

To be clear, my name’s not Fabiola. Woof.group is a community forum that runs on a shoestring budget. We can’t hire anyone for anything, and certainly not the templating mishap {{specific_hiring_initiative}}. This would be immediately obvious to anyone who did a moment’s research.

I was exhausted, and haunted by death, and these ridiculous slop-filled emails kept coming, week after week. Staring into the middle distance, I booked the meeting he asked for, intending to ask him politely to please stop emailing me. He canceled the meeting. I tried again. He canceled again.

The emails kept coming. I started calling him on the phone every time he sent an email. He never picked up. I was chatting with some friends about the emails—how I was at my wit’s end, how the whole thing was, and how many other people whose time he must be wasting. I asked if it would be reasonable and polite to write a physical letter to him asking him to stop sending spam. And someone suggested:

Too bad we don’t live in an age where you could take out a prominent newspaper ad in his home town paper

Another friend chimed in:

And you would be supporting a local newspaper

I called the ad manager of his local newspaper. It took a couple minutes to explain what was going on, I wanted to make sure it wouldn’t create any trouble for the paper, and she needed to run it by her team. But the answer came back, “yes”—and it was a lot cheaper than I thought. I got the dimensions and worked up an ad in Inkscape.

You know what? That worked! Haven’t gotten a single spam email from Tom since.

I can’t say this is time- or cost-effective. Mostly I just sigh and feed the email to the Bayesian filters, hoping they’ll catch it next time. But this spam caught me at an absurd, difficult time in my life, and in retrospect, I’m weirdly proud of what happened. Woof.group is tiny, which tells me that this campaign was likely casting a broad net. Somewhere out there, I bet there are thousands of people who were getting spam from Tom and rolling their eyes. I’d like to imagine that one day in July, the emails stopped for them too.

items.title: Announcing Hegel-clj
items.author: Aphyr
items.content:
I’ve just released hegel-clj, a Clojure interface for the Hegel generative testing library. You can jump right to the docs, but I thought it might be interesting to explain why I want another testing library.

I do a lot of generative testing in Clojure with the excellent test.check. However, using test.check can be frustrating! In particular, complex generators can get stuck during shrinking, leaving me trying to prune down a complex data structure by hand. The culprit is usually . If you’re not familiar with test.check, Quickcheck, or other libraries in this family, is a generator which draws some random value, then uses that to construct a generator, which in turn is used to draw some other value.

We can also write this using test.check’s macro, which expands to a series of nested s under the hood.

This leads to the canonical example of poor shrinking in test.check. Let’s try to find a vector containing :

That contain 42, but this vector is . Why are there all these zeroes? Once test.check found this vector, surely it could have shrunk it to just , right?

The answer has to do with shrink trees. Test.check generators don’t actually return values like . Instead they return a lazily evaluated tree of values: the root might be , and its children might be , and each of children has further children: has children , and so on. Simplifying a bit, here’s how the tree for large integers is defined:

So, if test.check finds that violates some property we’re testing, it tries the first child of , . Let’s say that passes the test, so test.check tries the next child of : . If fails, test.check tries its first child , and so on. By performing this depth-first search of the tree, and choosing the branches cleverly, test.check can often quickly shrink an integer to a smaller one that still fails the test.

A similar strategy applies to fixed-size vectors. The tree for a vector like has children like and , based on the trees for each individual element of the vector. This explains why test.check produced a vector like : it found something like [91 23 1034543 ... 42 15], then shrank the first element to zero, then the second, and so on. The only element it couldn’t shrink was the one that caused our property to fail: . Because our generator (tcg/vector tcg/large-integer size) always used a fixed , the tree for that vector always contained elements—in this case, 39.

Hang on! We didn’t just generate fixed-size vectors. We used to draw a size, then built a vector of that size:

What kind of trees does produce? The code involves some gnarly higher-order functions, but in essence ’s trees can shrink in two ways. They can shrink the outer value (the returned by ), or they can shrink the inner value (the vector returned by .

Now imagine draws a size of , then generates a vector of a hundred elements like . This contains , so test.check begins hunting through the shrink tree. One of the branches it can take shrinks the parameter, starting with . But if picks any of those sizes, the vector is useless—it’s the wrong size! So calls our function with to construct a generator of 50-element vectors, and generates a single vector from that generator. This vector will have random elements, like .

If there’s no in the vector of 50 elements, then test.check abandons that branch and moves on to size . It draws a new vector of 75 elements like , and since that contains , it can continue shrinking. But since is an uncommon integer, and test.check draws new elements for each , it is very likely that most sizes will not produce a vector with , and test.check will get stuck with, say, 39 elements. From there it can shrink each element, producing the comically oversized…

For this vector it’s fairly obvious what’s wrong. But for nontrivial test.check generators, there might be a dozen nested levels of with complex downstream consequences. Every one of them offers a place for test.check to get stuck, and the smallest failing case can be devilishly tricky to understand. Experienced test.check users try to avoid and —but they’re fundamentally inescapable for many problems.

Over in the Python world, the Hypothesis team took a very different approach to shrinking. Test.check is fundamentally a two-phase system: first it asks a generator to produce a shrink tree. Then, if the root of that tree looks “bad”, it explores the rest of that tree. Instead, Hypothesis generators produce a single value, and if that value looks bad, they re-run the generator and ask it to produce something similar, but smaller. This approach, called internal test-case-reduction, is the foundation of Hegel.

Hegel is a new cross-platform library for generative testing. It provides deterministic generators which draw random values from an imperative, structured RNG, as well as a rich family of special values and shrinking tactics. Writing these generators and shrinkers is hard. The idea is that Hegel’s core library will do this hard work once, and simpler wrapper libraries will extend the benefits of that hard work across many languages.

I’ve been working for a few months on hegel-clj, which offers Clojure bindings for Hegel, and I think it’s ready for the folks to try it out. To test something, you call , draw some values from generators, and throw an exception if the test fails. Hegel searches for values that make that body throw, then shrinks them.

,

The smallest case Hegel found involved a single draw of the number , which caused the assertion to throw.

Generators are pure, composable structures, just like in test.check. Here’s a few values drawn from a generator of booleans:

Or a map representing a person, with a name generated by a regular expression and an integer age:

, , , , ,

The higher-order combinators are all there too. You can transform generated values with :

Or build one generator out of another using :

Like test.check, we offer a macro which lets you bind both regular values or generators to variables; if the right-hand side is a generator, it draws a random value from it. And unlike test.check, these generators shrink well. Instead of thirty-nine elements, Hegel can find the much-shorter “bad” vector, .

,

With , if you want to thread multiple values through or , you have to build and destructure maps or tuples. Hegel-clj lets you lift arbitrary code into a generator using , which makes it easier to build complex generators:

, ,
  ,

You can build recursive generators with a promise-style API. The generator provides a blank space for a generator, which can be filled in later:

And best of all, ships with easy-to-use integration for clojure.test, making generative tests as easy as example-based ones:

,

It’s hard to log debugging output with test.check—you’ll have to sift through thousands of test runs with complex inputs, and many of those runs won’t actually trigger the bug you’re searching for. Hegel has the notion of a “final” test case: after it’s found a counterexample, and shrunk it to a smaller version, it comes back and re-runs that case as a part of the final phase. We can use to execute some debugging code only during these final cases, or and , which wrap and clojure.tools.logging/info respectively. I think there’s a bug in Hegel that causes it to run more final cases than it should, but it’s still a big step up.

Finally, test.check has been around for a while, and like many Clojure projects it has an exceptionally stable API. That’s great for compatibility, but it means some early choices are now fossilized. It’s , but . If you want an integer you have to remember the difference between , , , , , , , etc. Common generators require keyword arguments, like (large-integer* {:min 0, :max 10}). Some generators like are only callable with varargs, which makes composition tricky. The properties API feels a tad fussy. And many of the ergonomic features you want, like generating strings from a regular expression, or integration with clojure.test, require an extra library like test.chuck. Test.check is , but with the benefit of hindsight and a fresh canvas, I’ve tried to design a more streamlined, consistent, and approachable API.

I’ve used test.check for over a decade now and it’s one of my favorite things about Clojure. I want to thank Reid Draper, Gary Fredericks, Alex Miller, and everyone else who’s contributed to the library. I’m also indebted to David MacIver, Liam DeVoe, and Esau Rodriguez from the Hegel team at Antithesis. They took time to talk me through Hegel’s design, answered endless questions about the protocol, and helped fix a whole slew of issues that we found. Y’all rock.

I’m pleased to announce hegel-clj 0.1.1, and I’m starting to use it to test my own projects. I hope it will be useful for you too. ❤️

items.title: RIP, Harvest
items.author: Aphyr
items.content:
I’ve been a self-employed contractor for about a decade now, and I’m bummed about Harvest.

Harvest was a time-tracking and invoicing service. You’d track how many hours or weeks you spent on a project, put together an invoice, email it to the client, and close it out when they paid. There was a little Stripe integration for accepting credit and ACH payments on the invoice web view. A historical chart of total billed/paid amounts over time, and a table of invoices. Harvest was exactly what you want from small-business software: it solved a well-defined problem with a reliable, simple interface, and did so at a reasonable monthly price. They managed to avoid scope creep and never tried to become an accounting platform, or a blockchain for washing machines. I loved Harvest and raved about it to every self-employed person I met.

Back in 2025 Harvest got bought out by Bending Spoons, the company that gutted Vimeo. I was worried they might ruin it, but was busy with other things and didn’t have time to look for new invoicing software.

Long story short, they raised my price from $13.32 to $133.98 per month by moving everyone to a new “enterprise” plan and “unlimited” usage billing model, which is, as far as I can tell, exactly what I had before. There’s also a “flex” plan which costs $12.65 per month… but that plan now skims an additional 2% on top of the usual ~3% card transaction fees. To be clear, that 3% pays for the whole credit card network, plus all the people working at Stripe and Mastercard, plus the financial risk of chargebacks and fraud, etc. Harvest isn’t doing any of that work. I don’t know about you, but I don’t think I need to spend 2% of my gross revenue to send a couple PDFs a month and wrap a Stripe web form.

I wrote to Harvest about this, and discovered that they don’t read customer emails any more. Instead they have a Large Language Model repeatedly vomit thousands of words at you. I’m no stranger to enshittification, but man, I did not anticipate the speed at which Bending Spoons would drive a perfectly good company into the ground.

Time to find a new invoicing service, I guess. Maybe bookkeeping too—Intuit’s Quickbooks Online seems to have completely jumped the shark. Any of y’all freelancers have a system you like?
